t: Count Array Pairs Divisible by K: GCD Bucketing
o: We count index pairs (i, j) with i < j whose product nums[i] * nums[j] is divisible by k. In [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] with k = 2 exactly seven pairs work; with k = 5 and [1, 2, 3, 4] none do, since no element carries a factor of 5. Checking all pairs costs O(n^2) — about 10^10 operations at n = 10^5 — which is hopeless. The saving grace is that divisibility of a product by k depends only on each operand's gcd with k: a partner b works for a exactly when b is a multiple of k / gcd(a, k). Since gcd(x, k) is always a divisor of k, and k <= 10^5 has at most 128 divisors, all values collapse into a small number of classes whose combinations can be examined exhaustively.
k: a * b is divisible by k exactly when b is a multiple of k / gcd(a, k) — each element cares about partners only through its gcd with k.
gcd(x, k) is always a divisor of k, giving at most d(k) <= 128 distinct classes for k <= 10^5.
Combining classes pairwise must avoid double counting: distinct classes contribute cnt1 * cnt2 once, while a class paired with itself contributes C(cnt, 2).

a.n: Approach 1: Bucket by GCD and Combine Classes
a.i: Replace every value by g = gcd(value, k) and tally class sizes. Two elements multiply to a multiple of k iff g1 * g2 is divisible by k, because g captures exactly the k-relevant prime budget of each operand. With at most d(k) classes we can afford to test every unordered class pair: cross pairs multiply the two tallies, and a class paired with itself uses the combination count C(cnt, 2).
s: Build cnt[g] = number of elements with gcd(element, k) = g.
For each unordered pair of classes (including a class with itself), test whether g1 * g2 % k == 0.
Add cnt[g1] * cnt[g2] for distinct classes and cnt[g] * (cnt[g] - 1) / 2 when g1 == g2.
a.t: O(n log k + d(k)^2) — one Euclid per element, then pairwise checks over at most d(k) <= 128 classes.

a.n: Approach 2: Stream Elements Against a Divisor Census
a.i: Flip the viewpoint: process elements left to right, and for the current x compute need = k / gcd(x, k). Every earlier element divisible by need pairs validly with x, so maintain cnt[d] = how many processed elements are divisible by d and read cnt[need] before inserting x. Updating all divisor buckets of x costs O(sqrt(x)) through standard divisor-pair enumeration. This streaming formulation also works when elements arrive online.
s: Initialize an empty divisor-count map and the answer to 0.
For each x, first add cnt[k / gcd(x, k)] to the answer (pairs with strictly earlier elements).
Enumerate divisors d of x by trial division up to sqrt(x).
Increment cnt[d] and cnt[x / d], counting perfect squares once.
Return the answer after the sweep.
a.t: O(n * sqrt(A)) — trial-division divisor enumeration for every element dominates (A up to 10^5).
a.sp: O(A) — divisor buckets keyed by values up to A = max(nums[i], k).

w: Prefer Approach 1 in an interview: reducing everything to gcds with k and squaring at most 128 classes is both faster and easier to argue correct than streaming divisor updates. The two classic traps are returning a 32-bit type — the count can reach n(n-1)/2 ≈ 5 * 10^9 — and mishandling the diagonal of the class matrix, where a class must pair with itself via C(cnt, 2) rather than cnt^2. Verify against the samples: seven pairs for [1,2,3,4,5] with k = 2 and zero for k = 5. Natural extensions include counting triples whose product is divisible by k, or handling much larger k by factorizing it and walking divisor subsets.
